At the tea stall by the bus stand in their small town, Ganga was certain. "Farhan, the college fest was in March. It rained on the stage. I was wearing my green dupatta."
"It was February," Farhan said. "And it didn't rain."
"I'd bet my scooter on it." Ganga could picture every bit: water dripping from the tarpaulin, the wet plastic chairs.
Farhan scrolled through his phone and found a photo from the fest: the fourteenth of February, a clear blue sky, Ganga in a yellow dupatta, laughing.
Ganga stared at it. "But I can see the rain."
"Maybe that was sports day," Farhan said. "It poured then."
Ganga laughed, a little shaken. "I was so sure. Next time I'll check before I bet anything."

qa.q: What colour was Ganga's dupatta in the photo?
qa.a: In the photo Ganga is in a yellow dupatta, laughing.

qa.q: Why did Ganga feel sure enough to bet the scooter?
qa.a: Ganga felt confident because the dripping tarpaulin and wet chairs were so vivid that the memory felt like proof, even though it may have come from sports day.

qa.q: What does Ganga decide after seeing the photo, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To check before betting on anything, because feeling certain turned out not to mean being right.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel showing Ganga the photo?
qa.a: Farhan might feel a little awkward proving a friend wrong, which may be why he offers the sports day idea to soften it.

grounding: It shows a young adult certain about details of a college fest until a photo proves otherwise.

In a small café in Turin, Valentina tapped the table. "You booked the wrong train last summer, Mei. I remember your face when we missed it."
Mei shook her head. "I'm pretty sure it was you."
Valentina felt completely certain. She could still feel the heat on the platform and her irritation with Mei. "I would never book a six a.m. train. I hate mornings."
Mei opened their old messages and turned the phone around. There it was, from Valentina: "Booked! 6:05, cheap seats 🎉"
Valentina went red, then laughed. "I remembered being annoyed with you, so I remembered you doing it."
"Coffee's on you," Mei said, smiling.

qa.q: What did Valentina's old message say?
qa.a: It said, "Booked! 6:05, cheap seats," with a party emoji.

qa.q: Why was Valentina so sure Mei had booked the train?
qa.a: She remembered feeling irritated with Mei on the hot platform, and that feeling shaped the memory so that Mei became the one who booked it.

qa.q: What could Valentina do next time she feels certain about who did what?
qa.a: She could check the messages or other records first, as Mei did, before blaming anyone.

qa.q: What was it like for Mei to be blamed for the train?
qa.a: Mei was probably a bit annoyed but stayed calm, showing the message instead of arguing and then turning it into a joke about coffee. 🙂

grounding: It shows a young adult who is sure about a past detail until an old message proves her wrong.

At the hostel office counter, Rajni was firm. "I paid the mess fee on the fifth, in cash, to you. You wrote the receipt with a blue pen."
Vishal, the office assistant, pulled up the photo he takes of every receipt. It showed the eleventh, and her roommate's signature, not hers.
"That's not possible," Rajni said, and she meant it. She could picture the queue, the blue pen, even the fan clicking overhead.
"Maybe you came along with your roommate," Vishal said. "She paid for both of you on the eleventh."
Rajni phoned her roommate from the corridor. A pause, then laughter. It was true.
She came back, embarrassed. "I was so sure."
"Everyone is," Vishal said. "That's why I photograph the receipts."

qa.a: The photo showed the eleventh, with her roommate's signature.

qa.q: Why did Rajni say "That's not possible" and mean it?
qa.a: She could picture the queue, the blue pen and the clicking fan, and such vivid detail made the memory feel certain. 😳

qa.q: What habit of Vishal's settled the question, and what could Rajni borrow from it?
qa.a: Vishal photographs every receipt; Rajni could keep her own photos or notes of payments instead of relying on how sure she feels.

I owe you an apology, and a book.
When you asked about your statistics textbook last week, I was so sure. I told you I'd handed it back at the farewell party, in the corridor next to the notice board, and that you put it in your black backpack. I could see it. I even said, a bit rudely, "Check your own room first."
Yesterday I was scrolling through photos from the hostel move. There it is: me, two days after the farewell, sitting on my bed, and your textbook right there under my pillow, your name on the spine.
I was completely certain, and completely wrong. I'm sorry for making you think you'd lost it.
Coming to return it tomorrow, with samosas.
Parveen

passage: Nirmala, you want a story about being sure? Here's mine. I'm Gurpreet. Last winter my cousin got married in Patiala, and I was certain the wedding was on the fourteenth. Certain. I could picture the card: gold letters, fourteenth, a drawing of two elephants. I booked the night train for the thirteenth, told my professor I'd miss the fourteenth, and argued with my mother on the phone when she said, "Beta, check." "Mummy, I've seen the card." On the twelfth, my cousin sent a photo of the mehndi on her hands: "Tomorrow's the day!" I scrolled up. The card was right there in our family chat, and it said thirteenth. No elephants, just flowers. I caught the morning bus, arrived by evening, missed the pheras, and cried in the bus station. I still remember those elephants perfectly. They never existed.

qa.a: It said thirteenth.

qa.q: Why does Gurpreet still remember the elephants perfectly?
qa.a: The memory was built so confidently that it still feels vivid, even though the card had only flowers; the sureness stayed even after the facts changed.

qa.q: What choice could have saved the trip, and why?
qa.a: Checking the card in the family chat when Mummy said "Beta, check"; looking at the record would have beaten the confident picture in Gurpreet's head.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's mother feel remembering that phone argument?
qa.a: She may feel sad that her gentle advice was brushed aside, and sorry that her child missed the pheras and cried alone.

grounding: A young adult is sure of a wedding date and a card's design until the message in the family chat proves both wrong.

"You said you'd do the posters, Bhavna. At the meeting."
"I didn't. You did."
"I'm one hundred percent sure. You were sitting by the window and you said, 'I'll handle posters.'"
"I was by the window, yes. But you said it."
"No way. I remember your voice."
Bhavna scrolled through the phone. "Here. The minutes you typed yourself." Line four: 'Posters: Elizabeth.'
Elizabeth read it twice. "But I can hear you saying it."
"I believe you can hear it. Doesn't mean I said it."
Elizabeth laughed, half annoyed, half amazed. "My brain made that up."
"Brains do. That's why we write minutes."
"Fine. Posters are mine. Help me choose colours?"
"Deal."

qa.q: What did line four of the minutes say?
qa.a: 'Posters: Elizabeth.'

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth laugh, half annoyed and half amazed?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt annoyed and amazed at once, because the memory of Bhavna's voice felt completely real even though the minutes showed it was wrong.

qa.q: What does this suggest about settling disagreements over details?
qa.a: Check a record like the minutes, because feeling one hundred percent sure isn't proof.

qa.q: How did Bhavna handle the disagreement?
qa.a: Bhavna stayed calm, showed the minutes, and accepted that Elizabeth could 'hear' it without calling it a lie.

grounding: Shows a young adult confident about who volunteered for a task until written minutes prove otherwise.

passage:
Last month my college friends and I were arguing about our first-year trip to Goa. I was absolutely sure Rukmini had worn a yellow dress on the last night, when we sang on the beach. I could see it clearly, the colour, the frill on the sleeve.

"No, it was blue," Rukmini said.

"It was yellow. I'm certain."

She opened her phone and found the photo. Blue dress. Not even a little yellow.

I felt so silly. I would have bet anything on it. And I started wondering what else I'm totally sure about that isn't true.

I'm Sarita. These days, when I'm certain, I try to remember the blue dress.

qa.q: What colour was Rukmini's dress in the photo?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel when the photo showed a blue dress?
qa.a: Sarita felt silly and surprised, and a little unsettled about how certain the wrong memory had felt.

qa.q: What does Sarita do now, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: When feeling certain, Sarita remembers the blue dress, which helps keep in mind that confidence isn't proof.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have felt showing the photo?
qa.a: Rukmini may have felt amused, and maybe glad to settle the argument kindly.

grounding: A young adult is sure about a detail of a past trip until a photo proves otherwise, showing confidence isn't accuracy.

Hostel warden's note, Friday.

Seema, a second-year student, came to my office very upset. She was sure she had paid her mess fees on the first of the month, in cash, to Manjula at the counter. She described the day clearly: it was raining, and Manjula gave her a receipt.

Manjula said she did not remember it. I checked the register together with them. Seema's payment was recorded, but on the tenth, not the first, and by bank transfer.

Seema looked shocked. "But I remember the rain and the receipt!" I told her many people mix up days, and it doesn't mean she was lying. She apologised to Manjula, and they both laughed a little at the rain.

qa.q: On which day was Seema's payment recorded?
qa.a: On the tenth, not the first, and by bank transfer.

qa.q: How did Seema feel when the register showed a different date?
qa.a: She felt shocked, because her memory of the rain and receipt had felt so real and certain.

qa.q: What did the warden do well?
qa.a: The warden checked the register with both of them and reassured Seema that mixing up days isn't lying.

qa.q: How might Manjula have felt when Seema was so sure?
qa.a: Manjula probably felt uncomfortable and unsure, since she didn't remember the payment she was being told about.

grounding: A warden notes a young adult who is certain of a payment detail until the record shows otherwise; confidence isn't accuracy.

passage: The police form asked where the bike had been locked. "Outside the bakery on Kaptajn Street," Omar said at once, pen already moving. "I bought rye bread, came out, and it was gone." Olga, his flatmate, hesitated at the kitchen table of their Copenhagen flat. "Are you sure? Scroll up to Tuesday." Omar sighed but opened their chat. His own message from 9:40 that night read: "Locked bike at the station, walking home, so cold." No bakery. No rye bread. He stared at it. He could picture the bakery's glass door, the empty railing, the drop in his chest. "I remember it," he said slowly. "I really remember it." "You probably went to the bakery another day," Olga said. Omar crossed out the street, wrote the station instead, and felt his ears grow warm.

qa.q: Where did Omar's message say he had locked the bike?
qa.a: At the station.

qa.q: Why did Omar feel so sure it was the bakery?
qa.a: He could picture the glass door, the empty railing and the drop in his chest, so the vivid picture made him confident; seeing his own message left him embarrassed, with warm ears.

qa.q: What habit would help Omar after this?
qa.a: Check a record, such as a message or a receipt, before filling in anything official, especially when a memory feels very certain.

qa.q: What would have changed if Olga had stayed quiet?
qa.a: The form would have named the wrong place; Olga's simple question kept the report accurate without calling Omar a liar.
